idea.why: Genuinely multi-agent and matched to the problem: one specialist triages mail, one reads the day, a chief of staff merges, deduplicates and ranks. Crucially it stops the model at structured data and hands rendering to deterministic code, so the model never writes markup.

structure.why: Ten nodes, each the right type, one shared model feeding all three agents, a structured parser guaranteeing a renderable object, and a Code node doing the one thing no purpose-built node does well. Nothing is ceremony and nothing is a monolith.

connections.why: The weak dimension. The inbox read and the calendar read are wholly independent yet chained, so the schedule analyst waits on the inbox analyst for no reason; an inbox failure blocks the calendar branch entirely. The sub-node wiring is exemplary by contrast.

answer.why: End to end it is what was asked, rendered with table layout and inline styles so it survives mail clients. Empty-state strings, escaping and a fallback mean it degrades gracefully. Delivered by email rather than served at a URL, a defensible reading of presents but no way to open it on demand.

appraisal: The shape is right: three agents with distinct jobs, tools attached where they belong, and a hard boundary at the output parser so the model emits data and the Code node owns the markup, which is how you get a dashboard that renders the same way every morning. The HTML is better than most, escaped, inline-styled and table-based, with empty states for every section. The one real defect is the main chain: two independent fetches are serialised, so the calendar agent needlessly waits on the inbox agent and inherits its failure modes, and the merger prompt papers over it with a cross-node reference that only works because of that accidental ordering. A knowledgeable user would fan the trigger out to both analysts and rejoin with a Merge.
